issues.subcategory: extreme participant exclusion rate
issues.description: In Experiment 1, 17 out of 40 participants (42.5%) were excluded from the primary analysis due to having fewer than 10 high-confidence critical trials in one or more cells. This is an extraordinarily high exclusion rate that raises serious concerns about the representativeness of the remaining sample. The 23 included participants may systematically differ from excluded participants in ways that inflate the observed effects. The authors note that excluded participants had lower high-confidence rates (26.2% vs 53.8%), suggesting the included sample is biased toward participants who are more confident overall, which could artificially inflate the illusion rates since the entire analysis is conditioned on high-confidence responses.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (17 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the set size conditions.

issues.subcategory: extreme exclusion in Experiment 2
issues.description: In Experiment 2, 92 out of 290 participants (31.7%) were excluded due to insufficient high-confidence trials. This is again a very high exclusion rate. The systematic difference between included (49.2% high-confidence) and excluded (15.7% high-confidence) participants means the analysis is conducted on a highly selected subsample. The authors do not report whether the pattern of results holds for the full sample or whether the exclusion criterion was pre-registered. This selection bias could substantially inflate effect sizes and illusion rates.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) resulted in an inclusion of 198 participants (92 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the two color conditions.

issues.subcategory: confidence threshold operationalization conflates construct
issues.description: The entire theoretical argument rests on distinguishing 'memory illusions' (high-confidence false memories) from 'guesses.' However, the analysis is conditioned on participants rating their confidence as 4 (certainty) on a 4-point scale, and participants who rarely use this rating are excluded entirely. This creates a circular operationalization: the construct of 'illusory memory' is defined by high confidence, but the sample is selected to include only those who frequently use high confidence ratings. Furthermore, the 4-point scale conflates confidence in the memory with confidence in the response choice, and there is no validation that confidence 4 actually indexes a subjective sense of 'remembering' rather than simply a decision-making style.
issues.quote: Isolating high confidence responses is necessary to identify those responses that reflect a participant having an actual, albeit false, memory of perceiving something that was not there.

issues.subcategory: alternative explanation for time-based increase not ruled out
issues.description: The authors argue that an increase in illusion rates over time proves the illusions are memory-based rather than perceptual. However, an alternative explanation is that participants who are uncertain about their percept at encoding adopt a response strategy of defaulting to the real letter over time, not because the memory trace changes but because their decision criterion shifts. The authors attempt to rule this out by focusing on high-confidence responses, but confidence ratings themselves may shift over time (participants may become more confident in their default/expected response as the actual memory fades). The authors do not report whether confidence levels themselves change across delay conditions, which would be critical to evaluate this alternative.
issues.quote: If the frequency of reported illusions increases over time, then at least part of the illusions can be attributed to memory processing rather than perceptual encoding. After all, at both time points initial perceptual processing was finished, so if the illusions arose completely during perception, they ought not to increase over time.

issues.subcategory: absence of pre-registration for Experiments 1 and 2
issues.description: Experiments 1 and 2 do not mention any pre-registration. The stopping rules and sequential analysis procedures are only mentioned for Experiments 3 and 4. Given the large number of analytical decisions made (exclusion criteria, which interactions to report, collapsing over conditions after null results for cue color), the absence of pre-registration for the first two experiments raises concerns about analytic flexibility. The exclusion criterion of 10 high-confidence trials per cell appears post-hoc and is not justified theoretically.
issues.quote: Note that in this experiment the number of participants was determined based on a stopping rule implemented in an ongoing sequential analysis of the Bayes Factor for the critical t-test

issues.subcategory: figure reference error
issues.description: The results section of Experiment 4 refers to 'Figure 5' for the error rates, but Figure 5 was already used for Experiment 3. The correct figure for Experiment 4 results should be Figure 6. This is a clear internal inconsistency in figure numbering that suggests the manuscript was not carefully proofread and raises questions about whether the correct data are being described.
issues.quote: Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials.

issues.subcategory: inconsistent percentage reporting for Experiment 1
issues.description: In the Results section, the authors state illusory errors increased '7% increase from 19% in the short delay to 26% averaged over the short with interference and long delay.' However, in the Discussion of Experiment 1, they state 'From the Short...to the Long condition...or the Short with interference...the prevalence of high confidence expectation induced illusions increased from 29% to 39% and 43%.' These numbers are inconsistent: the Results section reports 19% for the short condition while the Discussion reports 29%. The Discussion also reports 43% for short-with-interference while the Results section states 26% as the average of the two non-short conditions. These discrepancies are not explained.
issues.quote: the increase in illusory errors (7% increase from 19% in the short delay to 26% averaged over the short with interference and long delay)... From the Short (memory probe 0.75 seconds after offset of the memory display with no visual interference) to the Long condition (memory probe after 3 seconds) or the Short with interference (memory probe after .75 seconds following an interfering display) the prevalence of high confidence expectation induced illusions increased from 29% to 39% and 43%

issues.subcategory: inconsistent illusion rate reporting across sections
issues.description: The Discussion of Experiment 1 states 'high confidence pseudo-to-real illusions (43%) were almost as prevalent as high confidence selections of the actual pseudo-target (50%)' for the short-with-interference condition. However, the Results section reports the overall illusion rate for pseudo-letter targets as 37% (not 43%), and the increase from short to long/interference as going from 29% to 41%. The General Discussion then states 'Illusory memories make up almost 20% of reports when memory is probed at 500 ms' which is inconsistent with the 29% figure reported in the Experiment 1 discussion for the short condition. These inconsistencies suggest the numbers reported in different sections may refer to different subsets of the data without clear explanation.
issues.quote: when the probe was after an interfering visual display, high confidence pseudo-to-real illusions (43%) were almost as prevalent as high confidence selections of the actual pseudo-target (50%)... Illusory memories make up almost 20% of reports when memory is probed at 500 ms

issues.subcategory: post-hoc collapsing over cue color condition
issues.description: In Experiment 2, the cue color manipulation (designed to test whether transiently induced expectations affect illusions) was a primary hypothesis. After finding no effect of cue color, the authors collapsed over this condition for all subsequent analyses. This post-hoc collapsing effectively doubles the sample size for the main analyses and removes a condition that was part of the original design. The decision to collapse was made after observing the data, which constitutes an undisclosed researcher degree of freedom. The authors should have pre-specified whether they would collapse over this factor.
issues.quote: First, we tested whether the cue colour influenced the occurrence of illusory errors... Because of this, in subsequent analyses all data are collapsed over the two cue types (red and blue).

issues.subcategory: online data collection confound in Experiment 4
issues.description: Experiment 4 was conducted online via Neurotask, while Experiments 1-3 were conducted in-person in controlled laboratory settings. This introduces a significant methodological confound: online participants used their own laptops with variable screen sizes, refresh rates, color calibration, and viewing distances. The 250ms stimulus presentation time is particularly sensitive to these variations, as different monitors have different refresh rates (60Hz vs 144Hz) and the actual display duration could vary substantially. The authors do not report any measures taken to control for these hardware differences, nor do they discuss this as a limitation.
issues.quote: the data was collected in an online experiment, using Neurotask scripting. Participants that signed up to take part in the experiment were invited to join a Zoom meeting at a preset time. Here, each participant was placed in a Zoom break-out room, and given the link to the Neurotask experiment, which they then started on their own laptop.

issues.subcategory: WEIRD and student sample
issues.description: All four experiments used undergraduate psychology students from the University of Amsterdam, primarily recruited for course credits. Experiments 2, 3, and 4 explicitly used first-year psychology students. This is a highly homogeneous WEIRD (Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) sample. The authors make broad claims about 'world knowledge' and 'prior expectations' shaping STM, but these effects may be specific to individuals with particular educational backgrounds or cultural exposure to the Latin alphabet. The generalizability to other populations, including those with different alphabetic systems or different levels of literacy, is not discussed.
issues.quote: The participants participated for student credits as part of a course within the first-year Psychology curriculum.

issues.subcategory: unbalanced trial proportions in Experiments 1 and 2
issues.description: In Experiment 1, real letter targets comprised 75% of trials and pseudo-letter targets only 25%. In Experiment 2, pseudo-letters made up 33% of targets. The authors acknowledge this imbalance and attempt to address it in Experiment 3, but the imbalance in Experiments 1 and 2 means that participants had substantially more practice with real letter targets, potentially creating differential familiarity with the task for the two target types. Furthermore, the response display in Experiment 1 did not always include both the target and its mirrored counterpart, creating asymmetric response options that could drive the observed asymmetry in illusion rates independently of world knowledge.
issues.quote: The target letter was a real letter in 75% of the trials and a pseudo-letter in the remaining 25%... If the target was a pseudo-letter, then it appeared as a response option randomly on half of those trials while on the other half of pseudo-letter trials only the real counterpart was one of the response options.

issues.subcategory: response bias alternative not fully ruled out
issues.description: The authors argue that the asymmetry between pseudo-to-real and real-to-pseudo illusions reflects world knowledge rather than response bias, based on the finding that the asymmetry is stronger in high-confidence than low-confidence trials. However, this argument is not fully convincing: a response bias could interact with confidence such that participants are more likely to confidently select a familiar (real) letter when uncertain, precisely because familiarity breeds confidence. The authors' own logic—that response biases should be stronger when memory is weak (low confidence)—assumes that response biases operate independently of confidence, which is not established. The comparison of high vs. low confidence trials is also not subjected to formal statistical testing.
issues.quote: if the illusory reports are actually not illusions, but due to response bias, then the pattern of responses that can be attributed to a response bias... should be present not only for the high-confidence responses; indeed, it should be even stronger for the low-confidence responses.

issues.subcategory: missing accuracy and correct response rates
issues.description: The manuscript focuses exclusively on error rates in high-confidence trials but does not report overall accuracy rates, the distribution of confidence ratings across conditions, or the proportion of trials that were high-confidence. Without knowing the base rates of high-confidence responses across conditions and target types, it is impossible to evaluate whether the reported error percentages reflect genuine changes in memory quality or simply changes in the use of the confidence scale. For example, if participants use high confidence more often in the long delay condition, the apparent increase in high-confidence errors could be artifactual.
issues.quote: For each memory delay (short, short with interference and long) and each target type (pseudo- and real letter targets) the occurrence of illusory errors (real-to-pseudo or pseudo-to-real errors) and other errors (selection of one of the unrelated distractor items) was calculated.

issues.subcategory: missing details on Bayesian prior specifications
issues.description: The Bayesian ANOVAs are conducted in JASP but the authors do not report the prior specifications used (e.g., the scale of the Cauchy prior on effect sizes for the repeated measures ANOVA). Bayes Factors are highly sensitive to prior choice, and without reporting these specifications, the analyses cannot be evaluated or replicated. This is a basic reporting requirement for Bayesian analyses.
issues.quote: The resulting data were analysed in a Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA in JASP 0.16.4, with the factors Target Type (real or pseudo-letter), Memory Delay (short, short with interference and long) and Error Type.

issues.subcategory: mischaracterization of fuzzy trace theory prediction
issues.description: The authors claim that 'FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should inhibit false memories' and use this to argue against FTT. However, this is a misapplication of FTT. FTT's similarity-based inhibition applies to the DRM paradigm where high similarity between studied items and lures inhibits false recognition because the lure is too similar to be discriminated from the studied item. In the current paradigm, the pseudo-letter and real letter are not semantically related items in a list but are visually mirror-image stimuli. FTT's predictions about visual similarity in this context are not straightforward, and the authors' dismissal of FTT based on this reasoning is not well-founded.
issues.quote: FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should inhibit false memories. This is not consistent with the current data: The mirrored counterpart (the real letter) and the target (the pseudo-letter) are extremely similar, yet false memories are abundant.

issues.subcategory: training exclusion only in Experiment 1
issues.description: Experiment 1 included a training phase with a 75% accuracy criterion for inclusion, which excluded 10% of participants. Experiments 2, 3, and 4 eliminated this training procedure entirely. This means that the participant samples across experiments are not comparable in terms of baseline visual memory ability. The authors justify this by saying only 10% were excluded in Experiment 1, but this does not address the possibility that the training itself affected performance in Experiment 1 by familiarizing participants with the task structure, potentially reducing the illusion rates in Experiment 1 relative to later experiments.
issues.quote: Since only 10% of participants were excluded from participating in the main experiment based on the training scores, the training procedure was not part of Experiments 2, 3 and 4 in order to not make the overall time on task too long.

issues.subcategory: Table 4 BFincl inconsistency with text
issues.description: Table 4 (Follow-up ANOVA for non-illusory error rates in Experiment 2) shows BFincl = 0.064 for Memory Delay, indicating evidence against including Memory Delay. However, the text states 'Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay).' This is a direct contradiction: the table shows BFincl = 0.064 (evidence against the effect) while the text reports BFincl = 190 (strong evidence for the effect). One of these values must be incorrect.
issues.quote: For other, non-illusory errors only Memory Delay was a relevant factor (BFm = 42... Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay)

issues.subcategory: interference display timing confound
issues.description: In Experiment 1, the irrelevant second display appears at different times relative to the memory probe depending on condition. In the Short condition, the second display appears 3.75 seconds after the probe; in the Long condition, 1.5 seconds after the probe; in the Short-with-interference condition, simultaneously with the probe. This means the three conditions differ not only in memory delay and interference but also in the temporal relationship between the probe and the interfering display. The authors cannot cleanly separate the effects of delay, interference, and probe-interference temporal proximity.
issues.quote: If the probe appeared 0.75 seconds after memory display offset, it either appeared together with the irrelevant second display (the Short-with-interference condition), or it appeared in isolation (the Short condition). If the probe was presented 3 seconds after offset of the memory display (the Long condition), it appeared in isolation. If the memory probe appeared in isolation (the Short and Long conditions), the irrelevant second display appeared 5 seconds after memory display offset

issues.subcategory: overclaim about all STM stages
issues.description: The authors claim their findings apply to 'all stages of STM' including working memory and fragile memory, and suggest implications for iconic memory. However, their shortest delay is 500ms, which is at the boundary of iconic memory. They explicitly acknowledge they did not test iconic memory. The claim that 'all stages of STM are susceptible to illusory memories' is therefore not supported by their data, which only covers the working memory and fragile memory timeframes.
issues.quote: Our findings suggest that illusory memories can occur during the WM and FM stages of STM... Our experiments currently do not test whether illusory memories arise in IM

issues.subcategory: inappropriate causal language for correlational time-course data
issues.description: The authors repeatedly use causal language such as 'world knowledge can shape memory,' 'expectations reshape perceptual representations,' and 'correctly encoded percepts of a pseudo-letter are being converted to illusory memories of a real letter.' However, the time-course data (comparing short vs. long delay conditions) is between-trial, not within-trial. The authors cannot observe the conversion process within a single trial; they can only observe that illusion rates differ between delay conditions. The causal claim that memories are actively 'converted' during the retention interval is not directly supported by the data.
issues.quote: correctly encoded percepts of a pseudo-letter are being converted to illusory memories of a real letter. So, perceptual illusions can, at best, account for a small number of incorrect responses, but memory illusions are also clearly present.

issues.subcategory: missing ethics approval details for Experiment 4
issues.description: Experiment 4 states that 'participants gave their informed consent online' and that the study 'was approved by the local ethics review board of the University of Amsterdam.' However, given that Experiment 4 was conducted entirely online during what appears to be the COVID-19 pandemic period (based on the Zoom-based data collection), it is unclear whether the ethics approval covered online data collection specifically, or whether a separate amendment was obtained. The consent procedure for online studies also differs from in-person studies and should be described in more detail.
issues.quote: All participants gave their informed consent online to participate in the study, which was approved by the local ethics review board of the University of Amsterdam.

issues.subcategory: missing information about letter set used
issues.description: The authors state that symmetrical letters (A, H, I, M, O, T, U, V, W, X, Y) were excluded, leaving asymmetrical letters as stimuli. However, they do not report the complete list of letters used, nor do they report whether certain letters were more likely to produce illusions than others. Different letters have different visual complexity and familiarity, and the specific letter set could substantially influence the results. This information is necessary for replication.
issues.quote: only letters that changed when mirrored were included in the experiment (i.e. the symmetrical letters A,H,I,M,O,T,U,V,W,X,Y were excluded from the memory and response displays)

issues.subcategory: lack of awareness check validity
issues.description: In Experiment 2, participants completed a questionnaire about the experiment's purpose, and the authors report that 'the relationship between the colour of the cue and the nature of the target was not mentioned in any of the responses.' However, the authors do not report whether participants were aware of the pseudo-letter vs. real letter manipulation itself, or whether they noticed the mirroring. If participants were aware that pseudo-letters were mirrored versions of real letters, this could influence their response strategies in ways that confound the world-knowledge interpretation. The awareness check is also not described for Experiments 1, 3, and 4.
issues.quote: Participants filled out a brief questionnaire in which they were invited to indicate what the experiment was about after the experiment. The relationship between the colour of the cue and the nature of the target was not mentioned in any of the responses.

issues.subcategory: BFincl notation inconsistency
issues.description: Throughout the manuscript, the authors use both 'BFincl' and 'BFinlc' (note the transposed letters) when referring to the same statistic. While this appears to be a typographical error, it creates ambiguity in a manuscript where precise statistical notation is critical. More importantly, the authors report BFincl values of 'infinity' (∞) in Table 2, which typically indicates numerical overflow in JASP rather than a true infinite Bayes Factor. These values should be reported as '>X' for some large value, or the authors should note that these represent computational limits.
issues.quote: Participants were more likely to select the mirrored (pseudo) counterpart of a target than to commit other types of errors (18% vs 11%, main effect of error type, BFinlc>1000)

issues.subcategory: feedback during experiment may reduce illusions
issues.description: In Experiments 1 and 2, participants received trial-by-trial feedback on their performance. This feedback could systematically reduce illusion rates by teaching participants to be more careful about distinguishing real from pseudo-letters. If participants learn from feedback to avoid pseudo-to-real errors, the illusion rates observed may underestimate the true effect. More importantly, the feedback creates a learning confound across the experiment: illusion rates may change over the course of the experiment not due to the experimental manipulations but due to feedback-driven learning. The authors do not report whether illusion rates changed across blocks.
issues.quote: Participants were instructed to report the letter that appeared at the cued location. They were explicitly instructed not to confuse real and pseudo-letters and received feedback on their performance after each trial.

issues.subcategory: predictive processing framework not uniquely supported
issues.description: The authors argue their results 'support a predictive processing view' of memory. However, the results are equally consistent with simpler accounts such as signal detection theory (pseudo-letters have weaker memory traces, leading to more liberal criterion use and more false alarms toward the familiar alternative) or associative memory models (real letters have stronger memory representations that compete with and override weaker pseudo-letter traces). The authors briefly mention these alternatives but do not design experiments to distinguish between predictive processing and these simpler accounts. The predictive processing framework is invoked as an explanatory framework but does not generate unique predictions that are tested.
issues.quote: Our findings support a predictive processing view of the formation and maintenance of memory in which all memory stages, including STM, involve integration of bottom-up memory input with top-down predictions, such that prior expectations can shape memory traces.

issues.subcategory: contradiction in Experiment 4 three-way interaction description
issues.description: In the Results of Experiment 4, the authors state 'There was a smaller increase in illusory errors from short to long delays when the target was mirrored (5% difference) compared to when the target was a real letter (4% difference).' This description implies pseudo-letter targets show a larger increase (5%) than real letter targets (4%), which would suggest the three-way interaction favors pseudo-letter targets being more sensitive to delay. However, the authors then say 'the best-fitting model did not include the three-way interaction' with BFincl = 0.45. The direction of the described effect (5% vs 4%) is also inconsistent with the overall pattern where pseudo-letter targets show larger illusion rates, yet the difference in delay sensitivity is described as being larger for pseudo-letters, which contradicts the claim that the three-way interaction is absent.
issues.quote: There was a smaller increase in illusory errors from short to long delays when the target was mirrored (5% difference) compared to when the target was a real letter (4% difference).

issues.subcategory: missing set size analysis in Experiment 1
issues.description: Experiment 1 used memory displays of either 6 or 8 letters, which is a within-experiment manipulation. The authors state that results were 'averaged across the set size conditions' for the exclusion criterion and presumably for all analyses. However, set size is known to affect working memory performance substantially, and the authors do not report whether illusion rates differed between set sizes 6 and 8. This is a missing analysis that could reveal important information about capacity limits and their relationship to illusion formation.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (17 participants were excluded) when the results were averaged across the set size conditions.

issues.subcategory: no control for verbal rehearsal strategies
issues.description: The stimuli are letters of the alphabet, which are highly verbalizable. Participants could use verbal rehearsal strategies (subvocal repetition) to maintain letter identities in working memory. Verbal rehearsal of a pseudo-letter (e.g., 'backwards C') might naturally convert to the real letter name ('C') during rehearsal, providing a verbal mechanism for the observed illusions that is entirely separate from visual memory processes. The authors do not control for or measure verbal rehearsal strategies, and do not include articulatory suppression conditions. This is a significant confound for the interpretation of the results as reflecting visual STM illusions.
issues.quote: All experiments rely on the extensive experience participants have with the alphabet. Previous experience with letters should have provided participants with abundant evidence that letters typically appear in their standard form.

issues.subcategory: unaddressed confound: differential decay rates
issues.description: The authors interpret the increase in illusions over time as evidence that world knowledge actively reshapes memory traces. However, an alternative explanation is that pseudo-letter memory traces simply decay faster than real letter traces (due to weaker encoding), and as the pseudo-letter trace decays, participants default to the most familiar alternative (the real letter). This differential decay account does not require active reshaping by world knowledge—it only requires that pseudo-letters are encoded less robustly. The authors acknowledge this alternative in the General Discussion but do not present data that can distinguish between active reshaping and passive differential decay.
issues.quote: An alternative to the idea that STM illusions are based on predictive processing, could be that the strong priors strengthen the encoding of the memory representation and make it less susceptible to decay.
